summary.text: Reducing the explicit binomial expansion modulo two gives terms indexed by triples satisfying \(m=n(k+1)+j(n+1)\), and the weight-preserving involution \((n,k,j)\mapsto(j+k,k,n-k)\) cancels every non-fixed pair. At a fixed point \(n=j+k\), the term is even when \(k<n\) because it contains the even central binomial factor \(\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}\); hence an odd sum requires \(k=n\) and \(j=0\), which makes \(m=n(n+1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{r\ge 0}x^r\frac{(1+x^r)^r}{(1+x^{r+1})^{r+1}}
   =\sum_{m\ge0}a(m)x^m.
\]
We prove that if the integer \(a(m)\) is odd, then \(m=n(n+1)\) for some \(n\ge0\).

First extract the coefficient of \(x^m\). For each \(n\ge0\), the binomial theorem and the negative-binomial expansion give
\[
(1+x^n)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^{nk}
\]
and
\[
(1+x^{n+1})^{-(n+1)}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\binom{n+j}{j}x^{(n+1)j}.
\]
After multiplication by the initial factor \(x^n\), the term indexed by \((n,k,j)\) has exponent
\[
n+nk+(n+1)j=n(k+1)+j(n+1)
\]
and coefficient
\[
(-1)^j\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}.
\]
For a fixed \(m\), only \(n\le m\) can occur, so the coefficient is the finite sum
\[
a(m)=
\sum_{\substack{n,k,j\ge0\\k\le n\\m=n(k+1)+j(n+1)}}
(-1)^j\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}.
\tag{1}
\]
Equivalently, once \(m,n,k\) are specified with \(k\le n\), the value of \(j\), if it exists, is uniquely
\[
j=\frac{m-n(k+1)}{n+1};
\]
it exists as a nonnegative integer precisely when \(n(k+1)\le m\) and \(n+1\) divides \(m-n(k+1)\).

We now work modulo \(2\). In characteristic two, \((-1)^j=1\), so (1) becomes
\[
a(m)\equiv
\sum_{\substack{n,k,j\ge0\\k\le n\\m=n(k+1)+j(n+1)}}
\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
\pmod2.
\tag{2}
\]
Call a triple satisfying the conditions in (2) admissible, and denote its unsigned binomial weight modulo \(2\) by
\[
W(n,k,j)=\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}\pmod2.
\]

Define a transformation on admissible triples by
\[
T(n,k,j)=(j+k,\,k,\,n-k).
\tag{3}
\]
This is well-defined because \(k\le n\), and the new second coordinate satisfies \(k\le j+k\). It also preserves the exponent \(m\). Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(j+k)(k+1)+(n-k)(j+k+1)\\
&\qquad=(j+k)(k+1)+(n-k)(j+k)+(n-k)\\
&\qquad=n(k+1)+j(n+1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]
Thus the transformed triple is again admissible for the same \(m\).

The transformation is an involution. If
\[
(n',k',j')=(j+k,k,n-k),
\]
then applying (3) again gives
\[
T(n',k',j')=(j'+k',k',n'-k')
=(n-k+k,k,j+k-k)=(n,k,j).
\tag{5}
\]

Moreover, the two members of each orbit have the same weight, in fact as ordinary integers and hence also modulo \(2\). The required binomial identity is
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
=
\binom{j+k}{k}\binom{n+j}{n-k}.
\tag{6}
\]
To verify it, both sides equal
\[
\frac{(n+j)!}{k!\,(n-k)!\,j!}.
\]
For the transformed triple, the weight is
\[
\binom{j+k}{k}
\binom{(j+k)+(n-k)}{n-k}
=
\binom{j+k}{k}\binom{n+j}{n-k},
\]
so (6) proves the assertion.

Partition the finite admissible set into orbits under \(T\). Every non-fixed orbit has exactly two elements, and by (6) those two elements have equal weights. Its total contribution modulo \(2\) is therefore
\[
W+W=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(m)\equiv
\sum_{\substack{(n,k,j)\text{ admissible}\\T(n,k,j)=(n,k,j)}}
W(n,k,j)
\pmod2.
\tag{7}
\]
It remains to analyze these fixed points.

Since \(T\) leaves the second coordinate \(k\) unchanged, (3) shows that a triple is fixed exactly when
\[
n=j+k,
\quad\text{equivalently}\quad
j=n-k.
\tag{8}
\]
There are two cases.

First suppose \(k<n\). Put
\[
D=n-k>0.
\]
At a fixed point, \(j=D\), and its weight is
\[
W(n,k,j)=\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
=\binom{k+D}{k}\binom{k+2D}{D}.
\tag{9}
\]
We use the identity
\[
\binom{k+D}{k}\binom{k+2D}{D}
=
\binom{2D}{D}\binom{k+2D}{2D}.
\tag{10}
\]
Again, this follows directly from factorials: both sides are
\[
\frac{(k+2D)!}{k!\,D!\,D!}.
\]
For every positive \(D\), the central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2D}{D}\) is even. Indeed, Pascal's identity gives
\[
\binom{2D}{D}
=
\binom{2D-1}{D-1}+\binom{2D-1}{D},
\]
and symmetry of binomial coefficients gives
\[
\binom{2D-1}{D}=\binom{2D-1}{D-1}.
\]
Thus
\[
\binom{2D}{D}=2\binom{2D-1}{D-1}.
\tag{11}
\]
By (9)--(11), every fixed point with \(k<n\) has even weight and hence contributes zero to (7).

The only fixed points that can contribute nontrivially modulo \(2\) must therefore have
\[
k=n.
\tag{12}
\]
Combining (12) with the fixed-point equation \(j=n-k\) from (8) gives
\[
j=0.
\tag{13}
\]
The admissibility equation for such a triple is then
\[
m=n(k+1)+j(n+1)
=n(n+1)+0
=n(n+1).
\tag{14}
\]

Finally, if \(a(m)\) is odd, its residue modulo \(2\) is \(1\), and in particular is nonzero. By (7), the sum of the fixed-point weights is therefore nonzero. After removing the zero contributions from all fixed points with \(k<n\), at least one fixed point with \(k=n\) must remain. Equations (13) and (14) then show that for this \(n\),
\[
\boxed{m=n(n+1)}.
\]
This includes \(n=0\), which gives \(m=0\), and proves the claimed one-way parity statement for all \(m\ge0\).
